title: Africa’s green hydrogen future: are we on the right path?
body:
Africa’s Hydrogen Strategy Is Too Export-Focused—and That’s a Problem

Africa’s green hydrogen debate is dominated by export narratives, shaped largely by external demand from Europe and Asia.

Exports matter. But an export-first strategy risks reproducing a familiar pattern: Africa supplying low-value green inputs while industrial value, jobs, and capabilities are created elsewhere.

What is missing is a clear focus on domestic demand and industrial integration.

- Green hydrogen can support Africa’s own steel, fertilizer, refining, transport, and power sectors—anchoring demand, accelerating decarbonization, and supporting structural transformation.
- Equally overlooked are opportunities in hydrogen-related manufacturing. Electrolysers, storage systems, power electronics, pipelines, and balance-of-plant components are where learning-by-doing, jobs, and technological capabilities are built. Yet these segments remain largely absent from discussions of Africa’s hydrogen future.

Without strong domestic demand, manufacturing linkages, and hydrogen-related manufacturing capabilities;

- Hydrogen risks becoming a new enclave sector: green in color, but extractive in structure.
- The absence of national or regional hydrogen-related manufacturing capabilities deepens technological dependence. In an era of intensifying geopolitical competition, as seen in ongoing US–China trade tensions, this should be a strategic concern.

A recalibrated approach would position green hydrogen as a dual-use industrial platform: enabling exports where Africa is competitive, while simultaneously building domestic markets and hydrogen-related manufacturing ecosystems.

- This requires aligning hydrogen strategies with industrial policy, public procurement, infrastructure planning, and skills development—rather than treating hydrogen as a narrow foreign-exchange opportunity.

The real question is not whether Africa can export green hydrogen, but whether it will use hydrogen to industrialize or simply export it to help others do so.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD Emmanuel Buadi Mensah
